title: Volatile Cedar
summary: Volatile Cedar, also tracked as Lebanese Cedar, is a long-running intrusion set that public reporting associates with Lebanon, though that attribution is generally described with limited or moderate confidence. The activity was documented publicly around 2015 against Middle East targets, and researchers reported a renewed wave of compromises in 2020 aimed at telecommunications and internet service providers across the region. Documented tooling includes custom remote access trojans and web server implants used to keep a foothold on public-facing hosts, together with exploitation of known vulnerabilities in widely used server and content management software. Reporting also describes reuse of publicly available offensive tools alongside the group's own malware. Defenders see it through modified server files, unexpected scheduled tasks, outbound connections from web servers and new administrative accounts on internet-facing systems.

beginner.definition: Volatile Cedar is a group of attackers that spies on telecom and internet companies. Reporting links the group to Lebanon, but researchers are careful and say they are not fully certain. It is also called Lebanese Cedar. The group puts hidden tools on public web servers so it can return later.
beginner.whyItMatters: Telecom and internet providers carry everyone's traffic, so a break-in there affects many people. This group stays quiet and keeps access for years. If a company ignores its web servers, attackers can hide inside them and watch email and network plans. Web servers are often forgotten because teams think of them as simple websites, not as valuable targets.
howItWorks: The attacker scans for public web servers that run old software with known weaknesses.
They exploit one of those weaknesses to place a small file on the server.
That file is a web shell, which lets the attacker run commands through the website.
They add extra tools, called implants, that run quietly and survive a restart.
They collect email, documents and network information from the company.
They keep several ways back in, in case one path is closed by the defenders.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk with an old key box behind the counter. A visitor notices that one hook is empty and nobody checks it. The visitor copies the master key and returns whenever the desk is quiet, sometimes through a side door that is also unchecked. Volatile Cedar picks web servers the same way. It finds the forgotten hook, makes a copy, and keeps coming back through more than one entrance.
takeaways: Public web servers need patching and file monitoring, not only a firewall in front.
Attackers keep several paths in, so removing one implant is rarely enough.
Attribution to a country is often uncertain, so describe the behaviour you can prove.

objectives: Explain what Volatile Cedar is and why its attribution is described cautiously.
Describe how web shells and implants provide persistence on public servers.
Explain why telecommunications providers are high-value espionage targets.
Recognise server-side evidence such as modified files and unexpected scheduled tasks.
Describe why attackers maintain multiple access paths in one network.
Summarise the patching and monitoring steps that reduce this exposure.
